text: The values on this sheet are the standards' recommended allowances (2006 NRC), practical concentrations (2026 AAFCO) or minimum recommended levels (FEDIAF Sept. 2025), and their maxs, or this application's own where a note says so; they are not all minimum requirements, despite this sheet's title and the "Requirement Name" label in D2 (see the L1 and G1 notes on the Standards sheet). The type of each max is coded in columns AU to BO (see the AU3 note).

AAFCO Large Breed Dog Growth: the 2026 AAFCO Growth and Reproduction profile for dogs with its lower calcium max, 4.5 g/Mcal (1.8% DM) instead of 6.25 g/Mcal (2.5% DM). The 2026 AAFCO applies this max to formulas that may be fed to large size puppies, those weighing 70 lb (about 31.8 kg) or more as mature lean adults (Footnote d, page 167; Footnote e, page 165), and, unless a product's labeling restricts it to specific breeds, to products bearing an All Life Stages claim based on being formulated to the Growth and Reproduction profile (page 170); for other life stages, including non-large-breed growth formulas, the calcium max is 6.25 g/Mcal (2.5% DM), as under AAFCO Dog Growth (Small & Medium) and Reproduction. Large size dog growth products and all life stages products substantiated by AAFCO feeding protocols using non-large size dogs must also contain no more than the large size calcium and phosphorus maxs (pages 162 and 186). In this sheet the two AAFCO dog growth selections differ only in this calcium max and in the energy min (this one covers growth only; see the AA4 note). The expected mature BW in E3 on the Standards sheet is not used by the AAFCO selections, so choose this selection for a puppy expected to weigh 70 lb (about 31.8 kg) or more as a lean adult, and for an All Life Stages dog food not restricted to specific breeds (see the O1 note on the Standards sheet).

Where 0.000000001 is added to a maximum in this column, it represents a 2006 NRC adult dog maintenance safe upper limit (SUL) given as a greater-than value; the amount added is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision. The same rule is used in columns F, N, V, X and AH. Used for sodium only: F60 = 15/4+0.000000001 (3.750000001 g/Mcal, from >15 g/kg DM in 2006 NRC Table 15-5). F61 = 0.4913 (the sodium MBW max derived from >15 g/kg DM; see the F61 note) carries no addition, as it is this sheet's own estimate, not a limit NRC prints. Iodine (F76, F77) has no addition, as NRC prints that SUL as >=4 mg/kg DM, not >4. A value equal to the limit itself is described as Highest (90% of Range or Greater) on the Standards sheet with or without the addition. Because the Standards sheet compares values at 7 decimal places, the addition does not change how any entered value is described. The MBW maximums in this column (F37, F39, F45, F61, F63, F77, F83, F85 and F87; F61, F63 and F77 are this sheet's estimates, see their notes) are kept as printed in 2006 NRC Table 15-5 per kg BW^0.75. The Standards sheet converts them with the energy in C11, so they equal the per Mcal SULs within about 4% only at 130 * BW^0.75 (the average laboratory or active dog type): e.g., the fat MBW max (10.8 g/kg BW^0.75) converts to about 83.1 g/Mcal at 130, but to 54 g/Mcal for the Great Dane type (200 * BW^0.75) and about 113.7 g/Mcal for the inactive type (95 * BW^0.75), against the 82.5 g/Mcal fat SUL in F36, and an intake entered in K4 moves it the same way. So for very active types a diet within the per Mcal SUL can read above the MBW row's max; per day, a dog eating 200 kcal/kg BW^0.75 at 82.5 g fat/Mcal takes in 16.5 g fat/kg BW^0.75, above NRC's 10.8. Table 15-5 Footnote b (page 360) asks for the per kg BW^0.75 amounts for dogs with an unusually low energy intake.

For FEDIAF Dog (MER 95 kcal/kg^0.75) and FEDIAF Dog (MER 110 kcal/kg^0.75): the MBW rows in these columns hold the FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-11 (page 58) minimums per kg BW^0.75 for adult dog maintenance, as printed; FEDIAF gives one adult dog column for both MERs. Units are converted where this sheet's unit differs (chloride 0.04 g = 40 mg, magnesium 0.02 g = 20 mg, cobalamin 0.92 mcg = 0.00092 mg); folic acid is divided by 0.6 to mcg DFE (=7.1/0.6), as on the folate row; and retinol is the vitamin A IU * 0.3, as on the retinol row. The Standards sheet converts them to per Mcal with the energy in C11: with no intake entered in K4 they give about this column's per Mcal values (e.g., protein 4.95 * 1,000/110 = 45 g/Mcal under MER 110), and with an intake entered in K4 they give the concentration FEDIAF calls for at that intake (FEDIAF section 7.2.5, pages 59-60: units/1,000 kcal = nutrient requirement per day per kg metabolic BW * 1,000 / energy intake per kg metabolic BW). Table VII-11 is rounded to 2 decimal places, so some converted values differ from the per Mcal values (e.g., sodium 0.03 * 1,000/95 = 0.3158 g/Mcal versus 0.29 g/Mcal; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). The Standards sheet checks each MBW row and its per Mcal row separately, so a diet meets both only when it meets the higher one. Table VII-11 gives minimums only. For the 13 MBW rows whose per Mcal row has a max (calcium, phosphorus, sodium, chloride, iron, copper, manganese, zinc, iodine, selenium, retinol, vitamin A and vitamin D), the MBW row's max in the MAX column is this application's own calculation, not a FEDIAF value: the per Mcal max * the MER / 1,000, the relation of FEDIAF section 7.2.5 applied to a max (e.g., vitamin D 800 * 95/1,000 = 76 IU/kg BW^0.75 under MER 95). With no intake entered in K4 it converts back to the per Mcal max, so both rows' ranges end at the same max; with an intake entered in K4 it converts to another concentration, as the min does, while the per Mcal row keeps FEDIAF's max at any intake. Its type is CALC (see the AU3 note): a value above it is described as Highest (90% of Range or Greater), and the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG does not call it excess. The other MBW rows have no max (range high 4 times the min). Fat MBW reads none: FEDIAF states that the fat minimum for a MER of 95 kcal/kg BW^0.75 has not been adjusted for energy intake (page 23), and Table VII-11's 1.51 g/kg BW^0.75 fits the MER 110 value only (13.75 * 0.110 = 1.5125). The Selenium, Se MBW row uses the dry diet value (5.20 mcg/kg BW^0.75) for every food; Table VII-11's wet diet value (6.40) is not used, as the Standards sheet has no Selenium, Se (For >12% Moisture Foods) MBW row (see its B91 note). So with an intake entered in K4 below the MER, a food of more than 12% moisture can be asked for up to about 19% less selenium than FEDIAF's wet diet value gives at that intake (5.20 versus 6.40): e.g., under MER 110 at 80 kcal/kg BW^0.75, FEDIAF's equation gives 80 mcg/Mcal for a wet diet (6.40 * 1,000/80), while this sheet asks 65 on the MBW row (5.20 * 1,000/80) and 57.5 on the >12% moisture per Mcal row. Up to version 18OCT26 these MBW cells read none.

Maximums in this column (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Tables III-3a and III-3b, pages 15 and 16): FEDIAF gives nutritional maximums (N) and EU legal maximums (L). This application uses the nutritional maximum wherever FEDIAF gives one, and the legal maximum only where it gives none; the sodium and chloride maximums are FEDIAF's Footnote c safe levels (see their notes). A legal maximum applies only when that trace element or vitamin is added to the recipe as an additive, and then to the total amount in the food; when it comes only from feed materials, the legal maximum does not apply, and only a nutritional maximum, where FEDIAF gives one, does (section 3.1.3, page 11). FEDIAF gives no nutritional maximum for copper, iodine, iron, manganese, selenium or zinc, so for these the legal maximum is used here for every diet, supplemented or not, as this application's cautious choice. FEDIAF gives the legal maximums per kg dry matter (DM) only, as they do not account for energy density (page 13); per 100 g DM: copper 2.80 mg, iodine 1.10 mg, iron 68.18 mg, manganese 17.00 mg, selenium 56.80 mcg and zinc 22.70 mg. This column converts them at 4 kcal ME/g DM (e.g., iron (681.8/(4*1000))*1000 = 170.45 mg/Mcal), so each equals the legal maximum only for a food of 4 kcal ME/g DM: for a food of 5 kcal ME/g DM the iron legal maximum is 136.36 mg/Mcal, and for a food of 3.5 kcal ME/g DM it is 194.8 mg/Mcal. To check a food against a legal maximum, compare its amount per kg DM. For vitamin D, FEDIAF gives both: this column uses the nutritional maximum, 800 IU/1,000 kcal ME (320 IU/100 g DM), which FEDIAF sets for growing giant breed dogs and recommends for the other life stages (page 26; it considers 425 IU/100 g DM safe for small breed puppies); when vitamin D is added as an additive, the EU legal maximum of 227 IU/100 g DM (567.5 IU/Mcal at 4 kcal ME/g DM) applies as well. The MBW rows' maximums in this column are not FEDIAF values: each is the per Mcal max in the row above * the MER / 1,000, calculated by this application (type CALC; see the I3 note).

For NRC RA Cat Maintenance (columns M and N): per 2006 NRC Table 15-12 Footnote c (page 367), the Amt/kg BW^0.67 values have been calculated for a lean cat with an energy intake of 100 * BWkg^0.67; for adult cats that are not lean, NRC calculates the amount of a nutrient as the energy requirement from Table 15-11 (see M4) multiplied by the Amt/1,000 kcal and divided by 1,000, which is what the per Mcal rows give. This sheet keeps the MBW values for both cat types: with the overweight equation (130 * BWkg^0.4), the MBW rows convert to about 1.12 to 1.35 times the per Mcal values for cats of 4 to 8 kg (0.769 * BWkg^0.27; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision), so for an overweight cat they ask more than the per Mcal rows. Per Footnote b, cats with an unusually low energy intake (below the suggested requirement) should be fed the Amt/kg BW^0.67 amounts, which the MBW rows give at the energy used on the Standards sheet (the calculated requirement, or an intake entered in K4).

Max type of each MAX cell in columns F to AT, one column per requirement in the same order (AU for column F, AV for H, and so on to BO for AT), on the same row; blank where that max is none. SUL = a 2006 NRC safe upper limit (SUL) as printed, per Mcal or converted by NRC's own unit factors. SUL> = a 2006 NRC SUL printed as a lower bound: a greater-than value, entered with the 0.000000001 addition, or, for adult dog iodine, ">= 4 mg" per kg DM, entered without it (see the F3, N3, V3, X3 and AH3 notes). SULm and SULm> = the same, per kg metabolic body weight (MBW), converted to per Mcal on the Standards sheet with the energy in C11, so their per Mcal value depends on body weight and energy (see the F3 note); no cell is coded SULm> in this version. SULm* = a 2006 NRC SUL per kg MBW that NRC states only for its reference animal, used here for every animal of that requirement: the MBW maximums of NRC RA Kitten Growth (column AH; see the AG3 note) and NRC RA Cat Peak Lactation (column AR; see the AQ3 note). PSM = a presumed safe maximum given in the 2006 NRC text, not in its tables (choline, page 233; see the F108 note). AAFCO = a 2026 AAFCO profile maximum. N = a FEDIAF Sept. 2025 nutritional maximum (N). N* = a FEDIAF nutritional maximum used beyond the life stage or animals it is stated for: the FEDIAF Dog Late Growth Ca:P max (AF56; see its note) and the FEDIAF Cat Reproduction arginine, methionine, tryptophan and Ca:P maximums, which FEDIAF Table III-4b states for growth (AT8, AT18, AT28 and AT56; see their notes). L = a FEDIAF Sept. 2025 EU legal maximum (L), given per kg dry matter and applying only to nutrients added as additives (FEDIAF page 11), converted here at 4 kcal ME/g DM (see the J3 and R3 notes). FSL = a FEDIAF safe level from a table footnote, not marked (N) or (L) (sodium and chloride; see their notes). EST = this application's own estimate (see the cell's note). CALC = calculated by this application from other limits (see the cell's formula; for the late gestation MBW maximums in column AP, see the AO3 note). Two more codes describe range highs set on the Standards sheet, not here: TPL = set by this application (see the row's notes there), and K = no max, the range high being the min times the multiplier in column K (see the K1 note there). A value above any range high is described as Highest (90% of Range or Greater) on the Standards sheet whatever the type, except a value entered under Min on a row with no min (see the E5 note there); the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG uses these types to decide when such a value is called excess (see the E5 note there): N*, SULm*, L and FSL are conditional, so a value above them is never called excess. When a max value or its basis changes, change its code in the same edit.

AAFCO's nutrient profiles set no energy requirement, so this sheet uses its own estimate, by one rule for the five AAFCO energy entries: the 2006 NRC maintenance energy by type of dog or cat for adult maintenance (G4, O4), Applied Veterinary Clinical Nutrition 2nd edition Box 3.1 (pages 46-47) for growth (Y4, AA4, AI4), and the 2006 NRC gestation and lactation equations for reproduction (Y4, AI4). For this selection the life stage selected in M3 on the Standards sheet decides which applies. Growth, from Box 3.1 (page 47; adapted from Thatcher et al. 2010): "Maintenance energy intake should be 3 * RER from weaning until 4 months of age. Thereafter energy intake should be reduced to 2 * RER until the puppy reaches adult size." With RER = 70 * BWkg^0.75, this is 3 * (70 * BWkg^0.75) with Growth: weaning to 4 months, and 2 * (70 * BWkg^0.75) with Growth: 4 months to adult size. Gestation and lactation, as under NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation (see AM4): with Gestation: weeks 1-4, the bitch's maintenance energy (the value in E4, for the type of adult dog selected in B4 on the Standards sheet, or 130 * BWkg^0.75 when no type is selected), as 2006 NRC Table 15-6 (page 361) adds gestation energy only from 4 weeks after mating (this sheet's reading); with Gestation: week 5 to birth or Lactation: bitch, the value in AM4 (Table 15-6, or Table 15-7 for lactation weeks 1 to 4, with its messages). With None, or a number of kittens, it shows "Standards Sheet Needs A Life Stage This Selection Covers". Up to version 18OCT26 this selection used 2.33 * (70*BWkg^0.75) for every animal, an average over the first 12 months counted from birth (4 mo * 3 = 12 plus 8 mo * 2 = 16 for a total of 28; 28/12 = 2.33), which matched neither growth phase and gave no gestation or lactation energy.

From the 2006 NRC; the life stage selected in M3 on the Standards sheet decides which equation applies. Late gestation (None, or Gestation: week 5 to birth), Table 15-6 Daily MER Requirements for Bitches in Late Gestation (4 Weeks After Mating Until Parturition) (page 361): maintenance + 26 * BWkg, where maintenance is the energy for the type of adult dog selected in B4 on the Standards sheet (the value in E4; Table 15-6 refers to Table 15-4, page 359, for variations in maintenance requirements, and 2006 NRC page 37 recommends calculating a pregnant bitch's energy from her individual maintenance requirement per kg BW^0.75 plus 26 kcal per kg BW), or NRC's average of 130 * BWkg^0.75 when no type is selected. Lactation (Lactation: bitch), Table 15-7 (page 361): 145 * BWkg^0.75 + BWkg * (24n + 12m) * L, where n is the number of puppies up to 4 and m the number from the 5th to the 8th, from the number of puppies nursing in G3 on the Standards sheet (no more than 8 counted; see the F3 note on the Standards sheet), and L = 0.75, 0.95, 1.1 and 1.2 in lactation weeks 1 to 4, looked up from the week in K3 on the Standards sheet (see the J3 note on the Standards sheet and the AN4 note). A missing number of puppies or week shows "Standards Sheet Needs Lactation Wk & Puppy #"; weeks 5 to 7 show "No NRC/FEDIAF Estimate After Lactation Wk 4: Use K4", as 2006 NRC page 38 gives no estimate beyond week 4: enter the bitch's intake in K4 on the Standards sheet. With Gestation: weeks 1-4, a growth phase or a number of kittens selected, it shows "Standards Sheet Needs A Life Stage This Selection Covers": this selection covers late gestation and lactation only (for a bitch in the first 4 weeks after mating, see NRC RA Dog Maintenance: this sheet's suggestion; Applied Veterinary Clinical Nutrition 2nd edition Box 3.1, page 46, states "During the first two-thirds of gestation, feed the bitch as a normal dog"). Up to version 18OCT26 this cell used 130 * BWkg^0.75 + 26 * BWkg for every bitch, whatever her dog type or stage.

From 2006 NRC Table 15-7 145*BWkg^0.75+BWkg * (24*number of puppies b/n1-4 +12*number of puppies b/n5-8) * correction factor for stage of lactation (L); Legend for Variable L: Week 1 Factor: 0.75; Week 2 Factor: 0.95; Week 3 Factor: 1.1; Week 4 Factor: 1.2; after week 4: no factor, as 2006 NRC page 38 gives no estimate beyond week 4 because milk yield varies considerably between individuals after 4 weeks of lactation. 2006 NRC pages 37-38 also show how the per-puppy terms are calculated: daily milk yield of about 1% of the bitch's body weight per puppy for puppies 1-4 and 0.5% for puppies 5-8 (no notable further increase above 8 puppies), times about 1.45 kcal gross energy (GE) per g of milk, divided by a 60% utilization of ME for milk production, gives NRC's 24 and 12 kcal ME per kg BW of the bitch per puppy (1% and 0.5% of BW are 10 and 5 g of milk per kg BW; NRC rounds 1.45/0.60 to 2.42, then 10 x 2.42 and 5 x 2.42 to 24 and 12; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). This equation is the energy min in AM4 when Lactation: bitch is selected in M3 on the Standards sheet, with the number of puppies nursing in G3 on the Standards sheet (no more than 8 counted) and the week of lactation (1 to 4) in K3 on the Standards sheet, from which L is looked up (see the AM4 note). Not used as a maximum: it is the peak lactation requirement, not an upper limit, and it can be lower than the late gestation minimum (e.g., for a 15 kg bitch with 1 puppy in week 1, about 1,375 kcal/day against 1,381 in late gestation at NRC's average maintenance), so this cell reads none and the energy range high is 1.55 times the minimum, as for every standard. Formula used here up to version 16OCT26: =(145*'Standards | Dyn Decile Sys Table'!B3^0.75)+('Standards | Dyn Decile Sys Table'!B3*((24*'Standards | Dyn Decile Sys Table'!G3)+(12*'Standards | Dyn Decile Sys Table'!I3)))*'Standards | Dyn Decile Sys Table'!K3
Per 2006 NRC Table 15-14 Footnote d that late gestation ME requirement = 140 * BWkg^0.67

The >12% moisture cut for wet diets or canned pet food is this application's own cautious choice, not a FEDIAF definition: page 13 of FEDIAF Sept. 2025 uses 12% moisture only as the basis of the EU legal maximums, and the FEDIAF glossary (pages 7 and 8) defines dry pet food as 14% moisture or less, semi-moist as 14% to less than 60% and wet as 60% or more. 12% moisture is used because it is a typical upper limit for dry (extruded) pet food made without humectants, to keep water activity low (industry experience; no published source). From 2006 NRC, Table 15-5 Footnote i 1 microgram cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) = 40 IU vitamin D3. Morris of UC Davis in 2002 showed that cats used vitamin D2 with an efficiency of 70% as compared to vitamin D3 (J Anim Physiol Anim Nutr (Berl). 2002; 86(7-8):229-38.). The 2006 NRC (page 201) states that in most species vitamin D3 is used with equal or greater efficiency than vitamin D2, citing cats, and does not state this for dogs; but it has been known since 1939 that dogs utilize vitamin D2 and D3 equally well (Arnold and Elvehjem, J Am Vet Med Assoc. 1939; 95:187-194.). In that first definitive study at the University of Wisconsin, growing dogs grew normally, with radiographic (x-ray) monitoring of bone development (if developmental abnormalities appeared) and blood calcium and phosphorus levels, over a five month experimental period. Later in 1943, Morgan and Shimotori of UC Berkeley showed that the same single massive IU dose of either vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 maintained blood calcium levels and vitamin D levels equivalently in growing dogs over the 180 day study (J Biol Chem. 1943; 147:189-200.). It is worth noting that in this study, it appeared that the vitamin D2 may have had a better lasting effect in the last couple of weeks compared to the vitamin D3 sources. Subsequently in 1947, Morgan with colleagues Hendricks and Freytag at UC Berkeley showed normal growth in control dogs over approximately 300 days when the same amount of vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 was fed as part of this vitamin D toxicity study (Am J Physiol. 1947; 149:319-332.). Finally the specific effects of vitamin D toxicity on the adult dog’s kidneys were studied in 1979 by Spangler, Gribble, and Lee at UC Davis. In this study, they used an overdose of vitamin D2 exclusively. This helped to further confirm that the utilization of vitamin D2 is not unique to growing dogs (Am J Vet Res. 1979; 40:73-83.). More recently, adult dogs fed a plant-based diet with vitamin D2 in place of D3 for 3 months maintained serum total vitamin D and bone mineralisation (Dodd et al., Br J Nutr. 2024; 131(3):391-405.). A supportive study in two client-owned dogs was also completed and selected by peers for oral presentation (Delaney SJ. No automatic adjustment is made to vitamin E concentrations for high PUFA diets which the 2006 NRC recommends increasing in high PUFA diets. See p. 208 for Table 8-2 and the Muggli 1994 proposed formula to calculate if of interest and/or sources of PUFAs requiring high amounts of additional vitamin E are not already fortified like fish oils rich in EPA and DHA. Also see the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K in Delaney and Dzanis 2018 DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537 . The 2026 AAFCO indicates for dogs (pages 165 and 167), "A diet containing 50 IU of vitamin E will have a ratio >=0.6:1 when the PUFA content is 83 grams or less. Diets containing more than 83 grams of PUFA should contain an additional 0.6 IU of vitamin E for every gram of PUFA." and for cats (pages 175 and 177), "Add 10 IU vitamin E above the minimum concentration for each gram of fish oil per kilogram of diet." AAFCO's dog figures of 50 IU and 83 grams are amounts per kg of dry matter: 50 IU/kg DM is its dog vitamin E minimum in the dry matter table (page 164), given as 12.5 IU per 1,000 kcal ME in its other table (page 166) at its presumed 4,000 kcal ME/kg DM, so 83 grams of PUFA per kg DM is about 20.8 g per 1,000 kcal ME. The 2006 NRC tables give vitamin E in mg alpha-tocopherol, with the footnote 1 IU = 1 mg all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (footnotes to Tables 15-3, 15-5, 15-8, 15-10, 15-12 and 15-14, pages 358, 360, 363, 365, 367 and 369, referring to its Chapter 8), and this sheet uses the NRC mg as IU one to one (this sheet's choice, following that footnote); for dogs this fits the 2006 NRC adequate intake of 24 IU per 4,000 kcal (page 209), the 6.0 mg per 1,000 kcal of Tables 15-3, 15-5 and 15-8 (pages 358, 360 and 363). In IU per mg, relative to all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (1.00), the 2006 NRC (page 207) gives all-rac-alpha-tocopherol 1.10, RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate 1.36, RRR-alpha-tocopherol (the naturally occurring form) 1.49, all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 0.89 and RRR-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 1.21 (United States Pharmacopeia 1985, largely from studies in rats; not measured in dogs or cats); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-14 (page 63) gives the same factors for the alcohol and acetate forms. On the Standards sheet, enter vitamin E in IU: multiply the mg of a stated form by its factor (e.g., 10 mg RRR-alpha-tocopherol is 14.9 IU). No vitamin E maximum is used on this sheet, as none of the three standards sets one, so on the Standards sheet the range high is the min times the column K multiplier (4) and values above it read Highest (90% of Range or Greater). The 2006 NRC states that there is no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs, that Hall et al. (2003) gave dogs 447 mg all-rac-tocopheryl acetate for 17 weeks with no adverse effects (no basis, such as per kg diet, is printed for this amount) and that the NRC (1987) suggested a maximum tolerable level of 1,000 to 2,000 IU/kg diet (page 209). For cats it reports dose-related toxicity of vitamin E injected into kittens from birth to 3 weeks of age (no deaths at about 20 mg/kg BW/day, significant mortality at 100 to 200 mg/kg BW/day and death of all kittens at 1,000 mg/kg BW/day; Phelps 1981; the 2006 NRC also describes the injected doses as about 50 to 1,000 mg/kg BW/day, a range the 20 mg/kg BW/day figure lies below: an inconsistency in NRC's text, kept here as printed) and prolonged clotting times, restored by vitamin K therapy, in cats fed fish-based diets fortified with vitamin E (Strieker et al. 1996), and it concludes that the data do not allow a safe upper limit of vitamin E to be defined (pages 209 and 210). The 2026 AAFCO records that the dog vitamin E maximum was deleted from its profiles because the 2006 NRC had set no safe upper limit, having no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs (page 173). See also Delaney and Dzanis 2018 on the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K (DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537).

Per 2006 NRC Table 15-14 Footnote d, late gestation requirements are calculated from the late gestation ME requirement of 140 * BWkg^0.67 (see AO4) multiplied by the Amt/1,000 kcal and divided by 1,000, so the late gestation mg/kgBW^0.67 value is the mg/Mcal value * 0.14: 1.44 mg/Mcal (see AO96) * 0.14 = 0.2016 mg/kgBW^0.67. The Table 15-14 value of 0.31 mg/kgBW^0.67 only applies to a 4 kg queen in peak lactation and is not used here. 2006 NRC Table 15-14 (page 369) prints 0.31 mg/kg BW^0.67 as the pantothenic acid RA for lactating queens, which fits its own 5.75 mg/kg DM (1.44 mg/1,000 kcal; see AQ96) at the Footnote d basis of a 4 kg queen in peak lactation with 3-4 kittens consuming 540 kcal ME/day (1.44 * 540 / 4^0.67 / 1,000 = 0.31); it is the 0.19 mg/1,000 kcal printed beside it that is the misprint (see AQ96). This value follows NRC's printed 0.31; up to version 18OCT26 this cell held 0.14, the adult maintenance value of Table 15-12, which is below the lactation MR of 0.25 mg/kg BW^0.67. Of this row and AQ96, the more protective value is used: the Standards sheet checks the two separately (this row converted to mg/Mcal with the queen's energy in C11), and a diet meets both only when it meets the higher one; for a queen eating less than the 540 kcal/day reference this row asks more than 1.44 mg/Mcal (e.g., about 2.5 mg/Mcal for a 4 kg queen with fewer than 3 kittens in week 1, about 318 kcal/day; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision).

NRC, AAFCO, and FEDIAF report "folic acid" requirements and not folate; 1 mcg DFE (dietary folate equivalent) = 1 mcg food folate per the US NIH (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Folate-HealthProfessional/ accessed 23SEP25); folate is the vitamin B9 water-soluble vitamin naturally present in foods. Per the NIH: "Folic acid is the fully oxidized monoglutamate form of the vitamin that is used in fortified foods and most dietary supplements." To convert to the common mcg DFE unit that covers all food and fortified/supplemental forms, one divides the Folic Acid value in mcg by 0.6 as 1 mcg DFE = 0.6 mcg folic acid when consumed with food. Every folic acid minimum on this sheet (2006 NRC, 2026 AAFCO and FEDIAF Sept. 2025) is converted this way, so each minimum here is the printed folic acid value expressed in mcg DFE: a diet whose folate comes from added folic acid meets it at the printed amount (e.g., the 2026 AAFCO cat minimum of 0.20 mg folic acid/1,000 kcal ME, page 177, is 333.3 mcg DFE/Mcal), while folate naturally present in foods counts one to one, so a diet relying on food folate needs 1.67 times the printed amount. The 2006 NRC states that its vitamin minimums are the bioavailable forms in the diet at the point of consumption, generally adequate when most of a vitamin comes from a vitamin premix, and that when a vitamin comes mainly from food ingredients the minimum should be modified by a suitable factor (Note on Bioavailability, page 356); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 bases its B vitamin minimums on bioavailable forms from a vitamin premix (pages 27 and 31). The 2026 AAFCO profiles give folic acid with no form or bioavailability basis (pages 166 and 177); AAFCO set its dog value equal to the 2006 NRC adequate intake (page 173) and kept its cat value at or above the 2006 NRC recommended allowance (page 179). The 0.6 comes from human nutrition (the NIH, above), and none of these standards gives a folate factor for dogs or cats, so dividing every folic acid minimum by 0.6 is this sheet's choice, the cautious one when folate comes from food. On the Standards sheet, enter folate as mcg DFE per Mcal: mcg food folate + (mcg folic acid / 0.6).

This is the adequate intake (AI) value as there is no basis for the higher Table 15-5 value of 425 mg/Mcal choline in the 2006 NRC, see page 233 in 2006 NRC where the allowance of 340 mg/Mcal is actually "recommended" for all life stages. AAFCO adopted the AI value in the 2016 revisions to its profiles after their thorough review of the NRC by their 2007 Canine Nutrition Expert Subcommittee (2026 AAFCO pages 167 and 173) and uses 340 mg/Mcal for all dog life stages (2026 AAFCO page 166); 2025 FEDIAF uses 409 mg/Mcal for their separately scaled 110 kcal/kg^0.75 (45 mg/kg BW^0.75, the same as the NRC AI, at that energy intake; 2025 FEDIAF Table III-3b, page 16, and Table VII-11, page 58), which typically would be higher than the NRC value. Therefore, the AI value of 340 mg/Mcal is used here, and the higher RA value of 425 mg/Mcal is considered erroneous/errant from the 2006 NRC 15-5 table. The same AI of 340 mg/Mcal is used for the other NRC dog selections in this sheet (NRC RA Puppy 4-14 Wk Growth, NRC RA Puppy 14 Wk+ Growth and NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation; U108, W108 and AM108), where 2006 NRC Tables 15-3 and 15-8 (pages 358 and 363) also print 340 mg/Mcal as the AI and 425 mg/Mcal as the RA; those three selections used the RA of 425 mg/Mcal up to version 18OCT26. For the choline max of the four NRC dog selections, see the F108 note.

Maximum 500 mg/Mcal for the four NRC dog requirements only (NRC RA Dog Maintenance, NRC RA Puppy 4-14 Wk Growth, NRC RA Puppy 14 Wk+ Growth and NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation); no NRC, AAFCO or FEDIAF table gives a choline maximum, and none is set for the AAFCO or FEDIAF requirements: 2006 NRC (page 233) proposes "a presumed safe maximum intake of 2,000 mg choline·kg-1 diet", converted here at 4,000 kcal ME/kg and used as an authoritative maximum until better safety data, including data with controls, are available. Note the inconsistency: the study NRC cites for this level, McKibbin et al. (1945), fed growing puppies 2,000 mg of choline chloride per kg of ration, as fed, which is about 1,490 mg choline/kg as fed or 373 mg/Mcal; that is the highest amount reported fed to dogs without a known issue, and it was in growing dogs. NRC (page 233) also notes that only Davis (1944a,b), with no control dogs, reported anemia in dogs given choline (Davis 1944, Am J Physiol 142:65-67 and 142:402-406; see also Davis 1947, Science 105:43-44), and that in pigs 2,000 mg/kg diet decreased weight gain when fed from weaning (Southern et al. 1986). No maximum is set for cats: NRC gives no choline safe upper limit for cats.

This MBW min of 45 mg/kg BW^0.75 converts to more than the 500 mg/Mcal choline max of this requirement (F108) when the energy used on the Standards sheet (C11) is below 90 kcal/kg BW^0.75 (45 * 1,000 / 500). That can only happen when an intake below 90 kcal/kg BW^0.75 is entered in K4 on the Standards sheet, as the energy calculated for every type of adult dog selectable in B4 there is at least 95 kcal/kg BW^0.75 (see E4); no diet can then meet both this row and the per Mcal max, and the Standards sheet shows both readings.
